segments.english: What does laughter mean? What lies at the bottom of the laughable?
What would one find in common between a clown's grimace, a play on words, a vaudeville mix-up, and a scene of refined comedy?
What distillation will give us the essence, always the same, from which so many different products borrow either their intrusive odor or their delicate perfume?

The greatest thinkers, from Aristotle on, have taken on this small problem, which always gives way under the effort, slips off, escapes, springs back up, an impertinent challenge flung at philosophical speculation.
Our excuse for approaching the problem in our turn is that we will not aim to confine the comic fantasy within a definition. We see in it, above all, something living.
We will treat it, however light it may be, with the respect owed to life. We will limit ourselves to watching it grow and blossom.

notes.text: Vaudeville here is the French genre of light stage comedy built on intrigue; keeping it preserves the cultural label. A plainer alternative, 'farce's mistaken-identity gag,' clarifies for Americans but loses the genre name.

notes.english_quote: What distillation will give us the essence
notes.text: Keeping 'distillation' literally preserves the image of one constant essence yielding many scents; 'intrusive' renders indiscrète as a smell lacking manners. Alternative: 'What process of extraction' would be plainer but lose the chemistry.

notes.source_quote: se dérobe sous l’effort, glisse, s’échappe, se redresse
notes.english_quote: gives way under the effort, slips off, escapes, springs back up
notes.text: Four unconnected verbs keep the sequence of evasions; 'gives way under' suggests ground yielding. 'Springs back up' approximates se redresse. Alternative: 'eludes, slides, escapes, rights itself' sounds more philosophical but less vivid.

notes.source_quote: enfermer la fantaisie comique dans une définition
notes.english_quote: confine the comic fantasy within a definition
notes.text: Fantaisie comique means playful comic imagination, set against definition and 'something living.' 'Fantasy' may suggest a genre; 'comic fancy' or 'whimsy' would stress play, though whimsy risks sounding trivial.
